analysis.one_liner: Cuts the monopoly period of a drug whose maker raises prices sharply.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would punish drug companies that sharply raise the price of a patented medicine by cutting short the government-granted monopoly period that keeps cheaper generic and biosimilar competitors off the market. A price increase of more than 10% in one year, 18% in two years, or 25% in three years would shave 180 days off the drug's market exclusivity, with bigger increases costing more time. Companies that raised prices could seek a waiver from the Health Secretary if they showed the increase was needed to keep making the drug.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and payers who face sudden, steep price increases on brand-name drugs; once the monopoly period shortens, generic and biosimilar makers can enter sooner and compete the price down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing sudden drug price hikes

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer that raises a drug's wholesale price by more than 10% in one year, 18% over two years, or 25% over three years loses 180 days of market exclusivity, with an extra 30 days lost for every 5% above those thresholds [S3].

The loss of exclusivity applies to the monopoly periods granted to brand-name drugs and to the 180-day exclusivity awarded to the first generic challenger, so sooner generic or biosimilar competition can bring prices down [S3].
Manufacturers must report qualifying price increases to the Health and Human Services Secretary within 30 days, and lose an additional 30 days of exclusivity for every day the report is late [S3].

The Health Secretary can waive or shrink the penalty if the manufacturer shows the price increase was necessary to keep producing the drug and does not restrict patient access or harm public health [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers, whose government-granted monopoly periods on high-price drugs would shrink; they keep less of the revenue from steep price increases.

drawbacks.text: The penalty only matters for drugs that still have market exclusivity left, so the oldest and most-gouged drugs are unaffected, and the Secretary's discretionary waiver could blunt the penalty in practice [S3].
The mechanism relies on manufacturers self-reporting their own price increases, with the additional 30-days-per-day penalty as the main enforcement stick [S3].

A fair objection: shorter monopoly periods mean less protected revenue for brand-name drugs, which manufacturers argue funds research on new medicines; the bill offers no answer to that trade-off beyond the waiver provision [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-known harm — steep price increases on drugs still shielded from competition — with a mechanism (earlier generic entry) that does not set prices directly, so it avoids some downsides of hard price caps. Its limits are real too: it reaches only drugs with exclusivity remaining, leans on manufacturer self-reporting, and leaves the waiver to the Secretary's discretion. On balance a modest but genuine consumer-protection tool that was never tested through the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee the day after introduction, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Golden introduced the bill on February 13, 2019, with five original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no further action of any kind was taken through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers keep their full monopoly periods and pricing freedom on existing drugs; patients facing steep price increases got no relief.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no recorded opposition exists; every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat (8 of 231 House Democrats, using 7 cosponsors plus the sponsor).

industries.note: The bill cuts 180 or more days off the monopoly period of any drug whose maker raises prices beyond the 10%/18%/25% thresholds, letting generics and biosimilars compete sooner. The industry's revenue from steep price hikes on still-protected drugs was directly at stake.
Earlier loss of brand-name exclusivity means earlier market entry for generic and biosimilar competitors, which profit when monopoly periods shorten.
